name: A slope that survives large numbers
brief:
Write `std::vector<double> slope_intercept(std::vector<double> xs, std::vector<double> ys)`. It returns `{slope, intercept}` of the least-squares line of `ys` on `xs`.

The $x$ values may sit near $10^9$. The formula from raw sums, $(n\sum xy - \sum x\sum y)/(n\sum xx - (\sum x)^2)$, has a zero denominator over a non-zero numerator there. It returns inf or NaN, never 0.5. Centre first. This is a depth option for firms that ask for C++ in a research round.
constraints: There are at least two points, and the $x$ values are not all equal.
hint: Compute the two means. Then add up $(x - \bar x)(y - \bar y)$ and $(x - \bar x)^2$. The slope is the first sum over the second, and the intercept is $\bar y - m \bar x$.

examples.name: Large offset
examples.why: Centre x first. The naive sums lose every digit and give inf or NaN.

tests.name: Two points
tests.why: A line through two points: slope 2, intercept 5.

tests.name: Large offset
tests.why: Centre x first. The naive sums lose every digit and give inf or NaN.

tests.name: Large offset, four points
tests.why: The same trick at $10^8$: slope 0.8, intercept -79,999,998.5.

tests.name: Unsorted points
tests.why: The order of the points does not matter.

tests.name: Constant y
tests.why: A flat line has slope 0 and intercept 7.

how: Submit runs 7 hidden tests. Each element is accepted when it is within relative 1e-9 of the expected value.
